before: Inferring gear microgeometry from transmission error requires distinguishing exact invisibility from weak sensitivity and operator discrepancy. We prove that nonnegative relief outside loaded support is exactly invisible under fixed geometry and compliance, including coupled tooth pairs. Synthetic likelihood and Monte Carlo studies show that nonzero local sensitivity does not guarantee reliable depth and start recovery. A 5% gain perturbation raises deeper-case median scaled error from 0.0916 to 1.86 across 200 paired realizations. Fixed-normal finite-element controls detect a dedendum signal while allowing compensating inverse profiles. A separate bilateral moving-contact model resolves 120 stations for three profiles at two resolutions, including 18 stations omitted by the earlier generator. Its fine-grid isolated, mean-removed dedendum signal is 0.243 µm RMS; the corresponding refinement difference is 0.015 µm. Equal-count inverse designs assess the added stations under nominal-elasticity approximation. Inverse estimates shift with reference resolution despite small transmission residuals. Discrete contact verification and selected independent-solver checks support operator-conditioned conclusions, without establishing continuum-converged reconstruction or physical profile recovery. The resulting protocol checks loaded support, numerical discrepancy and restricted alternatives before inversion.

after: Independent mechanical checks use CalculiX 2.23 [48]. The preceding six nominal controls (Table S34) differ from the bilateral entry approach by 0.100 and 0.0635 µm at two matched resolutions. These absolute differences are not negligible relative to the 0.243 µm full-cycle isolated RMS scale, but they are not errors of the isolated contrast. Additional paired addendum-only/combined profiles directly test that contrast (Table S39). At f=0.225, index 27 inside the former omitted block, the same assumed contours and body meshes as the fine cycle give 0.732 µm with hard mortar and 0.736 µm with the bilateral implementation, a signed difference of -0.00321 µm. At f=0.50 the contrasts are 0.185 and 0.182 µm. Subtracting the two phases cancels a constant offset per profile and gives 0.548 versus 0.554 µm, a difference of -0.00562 µm. before: The cross-operator experiments distinguish detecting a relief effect from reconstructing its geometry. The isolated 24/24 fixed-normal dedendum signal is close to the analytical prediction, but this agreement concerns an RMS response difference, not complete waveforms or inverse parameters. Restricted fits and profile objectives test compensating alternatives. In that historical study, bulk refinement stabilizes the isolated signal while substantial inverse-residual changes remain. Its 102 retained observations cannot establish insufficiency of all possible observations. Section 4.9 supplies a separate bilateral moving-contact generator at all 120 stations and tests equal-count designs including the former omissions. It retains closure and refinement discrepancies and explicitly measures the nominal-elasticity inverse approximation at the truth. These calculations do not retroactively change the historical fixed-normal data or certify continuum-converged inversion. Interpretation remains conditional on phase design, bounds, mesh, operator and objective scale; deterministic discrepancy prevents a nominal likelihood threshold from certifying physical confidence intervals.
after: The fixed-contact theorem and the updated-contact experiments concern different hypotheses. Propositions 1–2 guarantee invariance when nonnegative relief changes only gaps outside the loaded support while contact coordinates, normals and compliance remain fixed. Updating contact geometry or elastic stiffness removes that guarantee; violating a sufficient condition does not prove sensitivity, identifiability or the location where information must appear. The historical fixed-normal FE data in Section 4.5 admit compensating profiles. The separate generator and approximate inverse in Section 4.9 yield near-truth fine-reference point estimates for this virtual case, with reproducibility across the tested starts, but with design-dependent profile errors and remaining discretization/discrepancy dependence. This is compatible with the theorem, rather than a converse inferred from it. Several model features change together, so the comparisons do not isolate moving normals as the cause of improved numerical recovery. A small residual remains distinct from unique or physically validated geometry.

before: The results suggest three practical rules for inverse microgeometry work. First, compute the loaded-support range for the intended geometry, torque and phase grid: the sufficient condition can identify invariant relief sets in a fixed-compliance gap model. At sd=0.25, G2 has no loaded dedendum support and rank two, while G1 and G3 have appreciable dedendum sensitivity (Table 8). Second, a small transmission-error residual, nonzero tangent rank or close depth estimate does not by itself establish recovery of the relief shape; in the 24/24 test the near-true depth was one arbitrary value in an invariant fit set. Third, report a restricted addendum-only fit and the complete reconstructed profile together with parameter estimates and conditional uncertainty. Table 11 summarizes the scope of each evidence group.

before: The stress controls extend the numerical evidence to correlated noise, known and estimated covariance, periodic measurement errors, gain and a change of compliance formulation. With 200 paired deeper-case realizations, a 5% gain raises median scaled dedendum error from 0.0916 to 1.86; the 95% paired-bootstrap interval for the difference of medians is [1.44, 3.32]. Residual screening and noise-free transfer quantify consequences within the assumed operators, without establishing physical profile recovery. The defensible outcome remains an operator-conditioned account of observability and uncertainty, together with a pre-inversion support check. Independent mechanical and experimental validation remains necessary for physical reconstruction. The updated-contact experiment additionally provides a complete discrete cycle and equal-count transition controls, while leaving continuum-converged and physically measured parameter recovery unestablished.

before: Limitations and outlook. All inversions use synthetic data; the external amplitude reference is a published FE benchmark, not measured TE from gears with certified modifications. The analytical operator reduces each pair to one effective normal contact. All FE experiments are frictionless, quasistatic and plane-strain; dynamic effects, mounting deviations [17], wide-face effects [16] and the manufactured root fillet remain outside this reduction. Historical gap-only inverses retain fixed sections, normals and coordinates. Section 4.9 resolves the complete discrete cycle for the assumed contour with a separate full-geometry generator, but its moving-contact inverse retains nominal elasticity. Closure errors, two-grid changes and unsuccessful optimization attempts are reported; continuum-converged inversion is not established. Selected independent-solver checks validate neither the complete cycle nor physical relief recovery. The stress controls add periodic errors and known/estimated covariance under prescribed synthetic alternatives, without measured calibration. Future work should apply the support diagnostic to measured TE with certified relief, characterize fillet and face-width effects, and calibrate discrepancy before assigning physical uncertainty through a Bayesian framework [40,41]. Table S27 maps the original follow-ups; the discrete-cycle and periodic-error parts are now addressed conditionally, while physical validation remains open. A single deterministic FE difference does not identify a stochastic discrepancy covariance without replication or additional assumptions. The current archive also remains without a repository DOI.

before: As a screening diagnostic, Table S29 counts Q>146.567, the 95th percentile of χ² with 120 degrees of freedom. This compares against the known-truth noise budget without subtracting a fitted parameter count. Under a correct fixed covariance and exact minimization, fitting cannot increase the objective above its value at the admissible truth, making this a conservative screen; finite optimization can also trigger a flag. With incorrectly assumed covariance its nominal false-alarm interpretation does not apply, and no flag rate is assigned to FGLS. In the deeper 200-pair controls, 200/200 gain fits and 4/200 IID fits cross the screen. Thus the gain distortion is flagged in every computed fit in this control, including 14 nonconverged selections. This outcome is conditional on the declared operator, noise and finite search. A flag tests compatibility of operator, error model and optimization together, and does not identify the cause; passing it is not an identifiability certificate. The twelve external amplitudes cannot calibrate this waveform score or covariance.
